Carlos zipped his jacket to his chin, pulled his hat down over his ears, and stuffed his hands deep into his pockets before stepping outside.

What kind of weather is it outside? Name the detail that tells you.
items.answer: It is cold outside. Carlos zips his jacket to his chin, pulls his hat over his ears, and puts his hands in his pockets, which people do to stay warm.

steps: List the actions: zips jacket, pulls hat over ears, hands in pockets.
These are all ways to keep warm.
So the weather must be cold.

He "stayed at his desk" to finish his math.
Finishing first shows he is responsible and focused.

How does the puppy seem to feel? Support your answer with a detail.
items.answer: The puppy seems to feel guilty or afraid. It "pressed itself flat against the wall and would not meet his eyes," which is how someone acts when they know they did something wrong.

steps: The puppy chewed the couch and made a mess.
When Dad enters, it flattens itself and avoids his eyes.
Hiding and avoiding eyes suggests guilt or fear.

Mr. Okafor set a chipped teacup in the middle of the table. "This cup crossed the ocean with my mother," he said. "It is the only thing she carried from her old home." He wrapped it in cloth as gently as if it were made of glass and starlight.

Why is the cup important to Mr. Okafor? Use a detail from the text.
items.answer: The cup is important because it belonged to his mother and is the only thing she carried from her old home across the ocean. He handles it "as gently as if it were made of glass and starlight," showing how much it means to him.

steps: The cup "crossed the ocean" with his mother.
It is "the only thing she carried from her old home."
He wraps it gently, showing its value is in the memory, not the cup itself.

Every morning before school, Lena filled the bird feeder in the backyard. One cold week she was home sick, and the feeder sat empty. On the day she returned, she found a scattering of sunflower seeds on the windowsill, left there by her little brother, who had taken over the job.

What can you infer about Lena's little brother? Name the details that lead you there.
items.answer: You can infer that Lena's little brother is thoughtful and caring. While she was sick, he "had taken over the job" of feeding the birds and left seeds on the windowsill, doing her chore without being asked.

steps: Lena fills the feeder daily but got sick.
The brother left seeds and "had taken over the job."
Doing her task while she was sick shows he is thoughtful.

items.prompt:

The garden gate is rusted shut,
The roses grown to thorny walls.
Yet on the porch a lantern burns,
And someone waits inside the halls.

What can you infer about the house? Point to a detail in the poem.
items.answer: You can infer the house is old and neglected outside, but someone still lives there. The "rusted" gate and overgrown roses show neglect, while "a lantern burns" and "someone waits inside" show it is not abandoned.

steps: The gate is "rusted shut" and roses have "grown to thorny walls," showing age and neglect.
But "a lantern burns" and "someone waits inside."
So the house looks abandoned but is still lived in.

What does the students' nodding suggest about how Priya spoke? Cite a detail.
items.answer: It suggests Priya spoke fairly and respectfully, so even people who disagreed felt heard. She "repeated each person's point fairly before she gave her own," which is why even students who disagreed "nodded along."

steps: Priya did not raise her voice or interrupt.
She "repeated each person's point fairly."
Because she was fair, even those who disagreed nodded, showing respect for her way of speaking.

The old fisherman handed his youngest grandson the worn wooden oar. "My father carved this," he said, "and his father before him. It has pulled three families through storms." The boy wrapped both hands around the handle, feeling the smooth grooves where other hands had gripped it for years.

What does the oar represent to the family, and which details show it?
items.answer: The oar represents the family's history passed down through generations. The grandfather says it was carved by "my father" and "his father before him" and "pulled three families through storms," and the "smooth grooves where other hands had gripped it" show its long use.

steps: The oar was carved by earlier generations.
It "has pulled three families through storms."
The worn grooves from many hands show it is a family heirloom, not just a tool.

items.answer: You can infer Malik is a careful, thoughtful chess player who plans ahead. He "studied the chessboard for a long time" and "pulled his hand back" instead of rushing, and his small pawn move "three moves later" trapped the queen, showing he thinks several steps ahead.

Explain what the text reveals about Devi's character, citing the specific details that support your explanation.
items.answer: The text reveals Devi is determined and hardworking rather than resentful. She "did not slam her locker or complain," then "arrived early, stayed late, and asked the coach exactly which skills she needed to sharpen," and by midseason "her name was at the top of the list."

items.prompt:
Read the story.

The letter was written in shaky handwriting on thin, yellowed paper. It began, "By the time you read this, the orchard will be yours." In the margin, pressed flat and brown, was a single dried apple blossom. My grandfather had folded and unfolded this page so many times that the creases had worn nearly through.

Using details from the text, infer who wrote the letter and what it meant to the narrator's grandfather.
items.answer: You can infer the letter was written by someone older leaving the orchard to the narrator's grandfather, most likely a parent or relative, and that it meant a great deal to him. The "shaky handwriting" on "yellowed paper," the dried apple blossom, and the creases "worn nearly through" from being folded so often show he treasured and reread it.

steps: The writer leaves the orchard to the reader: "the orchard will be yours."
Shaky handwriting on yellowed paper suggests an older writer from long ago.
The grandfather wore the creases nearly through, so he reread and treasured it.

items.prompt:

At the shelter, most people walked past the oldest dog, a gray-muzzled hound who no longer jumped at the fence. Elias sat down on the concrete outside the kennel and read aloud from his book. The hound crept forward and rested its chin against the bars. "You just needed someone to sit still with you," Elias whispered.

What inference can you draw about why the hound came forward, and how do Elias's words and actions support it?
items.answer: You can infer the hound came forward because Elias offered calm, patient company instead of pressure. Unlike others who "walked past," Elias "sat down" and "read aloud," and the hound "crept forward and rested its chin against the bars," which his words "You just needed someone to sit still with you" explain.

steps: Others walked past, but Elias sat and read calmly.
The hound, ignored by others, crept forward to him.
Elias's line names the reason: the dog needed quiet, patient company.

items.prompt:
Read the story.

The championship trophy had sat in the school case for forty years, ever since the team's only title. Coach Barnes dusted it every Friday. When this year's team lost the final by a single point, the players trudged in with their heads down. Coach Barnes gathered them around the old trophy and said, "The team that won this played their whole lives to get here, just like you did tonight."

Write an explanation of what Coach Barnes wants his players to understand, and support it with at least two details from the text.
items.answer: Coach Barnes wants his players to understand that their effort and journey matter more than winning or losing this one game. He points to the old trophy, which he "dusted every Friday," and tells the discouraged players that the champions "played their whole lives to get here, just like you did tonight," comparing their effort to the honored team's.

steps: The players return "with their heads down" after a one-point loss.
Coach gathers them around a trophy he clearly values, dusting it weekly.
He compares their lifelong effort to the champions', so they value the journey, not just the score.
